raw_case_text:
A 20-year-old male with no prior medical diagnoses presented with a one-week history of worsening nonpruritic erythematous maculopapular skin rash which initially appeared on his face (Figure 1) and subsequently spread to his trunk (Figure 2) followed by his arms, legs, palms, and soles (Figure 3). At the onset of the rash, the patient reported associated headaches, photosensitivity, as well as intermittent fevers. Workup for viral meningitis yielded negative results, and the clinical picture was most consistent with a viral exanthem. He recovered spontaneously with slight resolution of the rash and, as a result, refused skin biopsy.
One month later, he presented once again with worsening of the same nonpruritic rash, associated with neck pain, photophobia, headache, low-back pain, fatigue, anorexia, as well as intermittent fevers with a peak temperature of 102F. Examination revealed generalized well-defined nonpruritic, nonblanching confluent targetoid papules and plaques (resembling EM) in various stages of healing. The lesions were located primarily on the torso, back, arms, legs, palms, soles, and lips. Newer lesions appeared erythematous, while older lesions appeared darker. The lesions located on the forearms and face were noted to exhibit small areas of fine scaling. There was no evidence of mucosal involvement.
In addition to the initial workup for infectious etiology and viral as well as bacterial meningitis (performed since the initial presentation was fever, photosensitivity, and headache), laboratory investigation revealed mild anemia (Hb 12.6 g/dL), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 75 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) of 11.05 mg/L, a positive ANA titer of >1 : 1280 with speckled pattern, a positive anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB titers of >8.0, and a positive RF of 34 IU/ml. Lupus anticoagulant antibody was positive (>44.4 sec), along with a low-positive anticardiolipin IgM antibody (>13 U/ml) and a negative beta-2 glycoprotein antibody. Anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, anti-Jo-1, anti-centromere, and anti-Scl-70 antibodies were negative. Serum chemistry and urinalysis were within normal limits. Hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex virus (HSV) 1 and 2, mycoplasma, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and parvovirus B19 were negative.
The patient then underwent a left arm skin biopsy, which demonstrated vacuolar interface dermatitis and positive colloidal iron stain suggestive of dermal mucin deposition, favoring the diagnosis of cutaneous collagen vascular disease.
Cutaneous lesions improved with administration of oral prednisolone.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male presented with a 1-week history of a worsening non-pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash spreading from his face to his trunk, extremities, palms, and soles accompanied by headache, photosensitivity, and intermittent fever, which relapsed 1 month later with targetoid erythema multiforme-like plaques, neck and low-back pain, photophobia, fatigue, anorexia, and fevers up to 102 °F.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially evaluated for a 1-week facial-to-acral maculopapular rash with headache, photosensitivity, and intermittent fevers (with a negative viral meningitis workup and spontaneous partial improvement), the patient re-presented 1 month later with a florid flare of non-pruritic targetoid papules and plaques across his torso, extremities, palms, soles, and lips alongside fevers to 102 °F, headache, photophobia, neck and low-back pain, anorexia, and fatigue.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for generalized non-pruritic targetoid skin rash, intermittent fever (102 °F), headache, photosensitivity/photophobia, neck and low-back pain, fatigue, and anorexia.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed generalized, well-defined, non-pruritic, non-blanching confluent targetoid papules and plaques (resembling erythema multiforme) in varying stages of healing across the face, forearms (with fine scaling), torso, back, legs, palms, soles, and vermilion lips, sparing the internal oral mucosa.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL), elevated ESR (75 mm/h), elevated CRP (11.05 mg/L), and normal serum chemistry and urinalysis. Autoimmune panel was strongly positive for speckled ANA (>1:1280), anti-Ro/SSA (>8.0), anti-La/SSB (>8.0), rheumatoid factor (34 IU/mL), lupus anticoagulant (>44.4 sec), and low-positive anticardiolipin IgM (>13 U/mL), while anti-beta-2 glycoprotein, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Jo-1, anti-centromere, and anti-Scl-70 were negative. Infectious workups for viral/bacterial meningitis, HBV, HCV, HSV-1/2, Mycoplasma, EBV, parvovirus B19, and HIV were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Left arm punch skin biopsy demonstrated vacuolar interface dermatitis and positive colloidal iron staining confirming dermal mucin deposition consistent with cutaneous lupus erythematosus / Rowell syndrome.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Rowell syndrome (cutaneous/systemic lupus erythematosus with erythema multiforme-like targetoid lesions, speckled ANA >1:1280, positive anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB >8.0, positive rheumatoid factor 34 IU/mL, and lupus anticoagulant positivity) in an HIV-negative 20-year-old male, confirmed by vacuolar interface dermatitis and colloidal iron-positive dermal mucin on skin biopsy. Administration of oral prednisolone resulted in prompt improvement of the cutaneous lesions and systemic symptoms.
